https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2025/09.title: Badenoch: We won’t be cowed by climate change ‘bullies’
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2025/09.subtitle: Tory leader criticises Labour for yielding to environment activists on North Sea oil, calling area a ‘graveyard for investment’
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2025/09.text:
Kemi Badenoch has vowed to take on “bullying” climate change activists after blaming them for halting North Sea oil and gas exploration with legal challenges.
The Tory leader said the planning system for new fields had “become a paradise for activists and a graveyard for investment”.
Speaking to oil and gas leaders at a conference in Aberdeen, she said “endless legal challenges” by environmental groups were blocking projects.
Mrs Badenoch accused Sir Keir Starmer of having “surrendered to the activists” over two of the largest fields in development, Rosebank and Jackdaw.
But she said a Tory government would ensure “no more judicial overreach” and pledged to introduce a presumption in favour of new fields getting the green light.
She described Labour’s decision to ban oil and gas licences for new fields as “unilateral economic disarmament dressed up as virtue” and pledged: “Conservatives will not be bullied by activists.”
Unless more investment is made now, she warned that the UK would be “reliant on imports for more than 80 per cent of oil and gas demand by 2030.”
Her intervention came after she pledged at the weekend to extract as much oil and gas from the North Sea as possible, arguing that economic growth and the national interest must come before net-zero targets.
However, a court ruled in January that consent for the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields had been granted unlawfully and their owners must seek fresh approval from the UK Government before production can begin.
Lord Ericht said a more detailed assessment of the fields’ environmental impact was required, taking into account the effect on the climate of burning any fossil fuels extracted.
The written judgment on the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields came after a case brought by environmental campaigners, Uplift and Greenpeace, at the Court of Session in Edinburgh. Labour ministers decided not to challenge the judicial review action.
Shell’s Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea was originally approved by the Conservative government and the industry regulator in the summer 2022.
Permission for the huge Rosebank oil development, 80 miles west of Shetland in the North Atlantic, was granted in autumn 2023.
This is the UK’s largest untapped field and Tory ministers argued the move would protect the UK’s energy security during the transition to net zero and create hundreds of jobs.
Speaking at the SPE Offshore Europe conference, Mrs Badenoch said: “Right now, the regulatory system is strangling the North Sea. We have more lawyers trying to stop oil and gas than rigs producing it.
“We need to overhaul the planning system for the North Sea because, let’s be honest, it has become a paradise for activists and a graveyard for investment.
“Endless legal challenges, funded by campaign groups, are blocking the very oil and gas projects we need to keep our economy alive.”
She said Sir Keir had “no answer” when she challenged him at Prime Minister’s Questions for why the Government had not contested the Rosebank case.
“Even now, Labour still refuses to commit to granting new licences at all. They are on the wrong side, standing with campaigning lawyers against British workers,” she said.
“Rosebank and Jackdaw could have powered millions of homes. But Labour dropped the appeal and surrendered to the activists. That was a political choice, and it cost Britain dearly.”
She pledged this “lawfare” would end with the next Tory government, but warned that without urgent action, 180 out of 280 fields will shut down in the next five years.
Mrs Badenoch said: “This is not a managed transition. This is collapse. Ed Miliband and Keir Starmer are not planning for decades ahead.
“We are killing this industry now, and if they succeed, they will not just destroy jobs in Aberdeen, but they will destroy our country’s ability to stand on its own two feet.”
Michael Shanks, however, a Scottish Labour MP and Energy Minister, used his speech to the conference to deliver a coded attack on her oil and gas policy announcements this week.
He said: “What drives us is a refusal to accept the status quo of the last decade, let down by a government that talked big but allowed thousands upon thousands of jobs to be lost from this industry and countries to steal a march on winning the jobs of the future.
“It’s easy to stick a few lines in a political press release and call it policy, but the hard work of stewarding the future of this industry is far too complicated for that.
“North Sea workers and this community deserve a government that says it’s time to invest in the future and manage this transition in a rational, cooperative way.”
Ami McCarthy, Greenpeace UK’s head of politics, said: “Kemi may be spending a lot of time reading the lines of Trump and Farage, but what she is clearly not reading is the science or economic advice of experts.
“North Sea reserves are drying up and what’s left and untapped is barely enough to keep it on life support – lasting no more than a few months or years at current rates of consumption.”
Also on Tuesday, Ms Badenoch addressed Tory MSP Graham Simpson’s defection to Reform UK.
She said: “If there are people who join other parties because they think they have a better chance of winning, that means they’re doing this for the wrong reasons.”
The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, Uplift and Greenpeace were approached for comment.

image.caption: Kemi Badenoch visits Aberdeen, where she pledged to maximise the North Sea’s resources
Protesters against the Rosebank oil project got their way when the consent for it was declared unlawful in January

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.title: Why Starmer’s nuclear ‘golden age’ risks becoming a lot of hot air
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.subtitle: Crippling costs and mountains of red tape threaten to pour cold water on the PM’s ambitions
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.text:
Donald Trump hasn’t been shy about criticising British energy policy under Labour, lashing out at “ugly” wind farms and crippling taxes on North Sea oil and gas.
Yet one area where the US president and Sir Keir Starmer seem to fervently agree is on nuclear power.
This week, the US and UK governments promised to work together to deliver a “golden age” of privately-financed power plant construction.
The agreement will see the two countries fast-track the approval of new, cutting-edge reactor designs by recognising each other’s safety regimes – a controversial move that has already raised the hackles of activists.
But to underline the economic prize on offer, the announcement featured a string of eye-catching investments being looked at by American and British companies with plans for fleets of reactors that will power the grid, as well as high-tech data centres needed for artificial intelligence (AI) software.
British Gas owner Centrica and X-energy, a nuclear start-up backed by Amazon, said they were exploring building up to 80 advanced modular reactors (AMRs) capable of delivering electricity and heat to both industrial businesses and millions of homes.
Meanwhile, Holtec International and the UK arm of EDF are looking at building a small modular reactor (SMR) on the former site of a coal power plant in Nottinghamshire.
Micro-reactor firm Last Energy is also exploring plans to power the London Gateway port, while Bill Gates-backed TerraPower is scouting out locations for mini power plants as well.
On the face of it, the deals looked like a major triumph for the Prime Minister.
But industry veterans were quick to note that, in their current form, they are just loosely-worded commitments, with the companies yet to sign binding contracts or exchange serious sums of cash.
Can Starmer actually deliver?
One potential blueprint may lie in a new report by pro-growth campaign group Britain Remade, which argues that nuclear power can offer “abundant, clean, reliable electricity” and lower bills for consumers – but only if the Government overhauls red tape that is “not fit for purpose”.
“US firms want to build here,” says Sam Dumitriu, the report’s author. “But turning it into shovels in the ground, data centres online, on time and on budget, depends on making the UK a lower-cost, faster place to build.”
Unlike wind and solar, nuclear offers round-the-clock power. It also takes up a tiny fraction of the space for the same output, meaning it has a smaller impact on natural landscapes.
That should make it an attractive proposition as the UK races to decarbonise its power system. However, Britain is now “the most expensive place in the world to build nuclear power stations”, Dumitriu’s research found – and by some margin.
That is because Hinkley Point C – the plant currently being built in Somerset by EDF – is projected to cost a whopping £46bn, or more than £12m per megawatt.
This is much worse than other reactors recently built by state-owned companies in South Korea and China (completed at a cost of around £2m per megawatt).
But it is also abysmal when compared to other plants built by EDF that used the same reactor design in France and Finland, which came in at around £7m and £6m per megawatt respectively.
Why is Britain so uniquely bad?
“It’s expensive to build pretty much anything in Britain,” says Dumitriu, who has previously highlighted how planning rules have made it up to eight times more expensive to build rail and road projects here than in Europe.
Hinkley Point C required an “environmental statement” that ran to more than 30,000 pages.
To prevent fish in the Bristol Channel from being sucked into the plant’s cooling pipes, EDF was forced to draw up designs for an “acoustic fish deterrent”: underwater loudspeakers that blast out noise and were quickly derided as a “fish disco” by nuclear advocates.
At the same time, Dumitriu claims the Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR) is stuck enforcing a regime that often “gold plates” safety standards unnecessarily and at enormous cost.
Under the “as low as reasonably practicable’” (Alarp) framework, companies must demonstrate that their designs are as safe as they can be rather than simply “safe enough”.
“It’s sensible in theory,” explains Dumitriu. “But in practice, for nuclear, it is driving bespoke features and long safety cases, all to avoid trivial doses of radiation.”
In one example of how this policy can gum up the system, GE Hitachi wanted to build a reactor in Anglesey, Wales, that was already proven in Japan. But regulators told the company it would have to make costly design changes to its ventilation system – all to cut radiation exposure by 0.0001 millisieverts, equivalent to eating a single banana.
Dumitriu says radiation “is a scary word” but that the amounts being quibbled over must be put in perspective.
The average worker in a nuclear plant is exposed to 0.18 millisieverts per year – slightly more than you would absorb by taking two transatlantic flights or eating about 2kg of Brazil nuts, according to the UK Health Security Agency.
A nuclear industry insider also complains that it is not always clear what planning authorities and regulators want. Officials often refuse to give explicit guidance to developers on how to address their concerns, for fear of being accused of bias if their decisions are later challenged in the courts.
“The current framework makes it very hard for any regulator to take a view on something,” the insider says. “And if you’re proposing new designs you need them to, at some point, take a view.”
Dumitriu’s report argues that the ONR should explicitly state its minimum requirements to give developers certainty about what they need to do. He also says the regulator should be forced to show that any design changes it requests beyond this are worth the extra money.
Starmer’s pledge to align with US regulators will potentially force the ONR to accept safety assessments by its American counterpart, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).
This could speed up the approvals process significantly – but also expose the Government to political controversy.
In the US, Trump has initiated a radical overhaul of the NRC which has unnerved some safety experts.
He has accused the NRC of “risk aversion”, fired several independent directors and ordered it to speed up the approvals of cutting-edge mini reactors in a bid to cement US “energy dominance”.
“There are good reasons why you need to maintain nuclear safety at higher standards, because the same level of extensive risk is simply not there in other kinds of projects,” argues Doug Parr, chief scientist at Greenpeace UK.
“Regulators need to be satisfied that the US nuclear watchdog under Donald Trump is as satisfactory as the tradition of quality regulation that we have here in Britain. At the moment, that’s quite difficult to believe.”
In another bad omen, Labour’s flagship reforms to the planning system are facing a revolt from MPs, peers and wildlife charities as ministers attempt to steer the legislation through Parliament.
Still, nuclear companies have noted the Prime Minister’s enthusiasm and there remains plenty of goodwill.
Decisions to fund the Sizewell C nuclear plant in Suffolk and mini-reactors designed by Rolls-Royce, in particular, have buoyed hopes that the Government is serious about its nuclear renaissance.
But there remains no clear route to market for privately-financed reactors.
To fix this, the Britain Remade report suggests ministers should offer SMRs and other mini reactors contracts for difference (CfD) subsidies of the kind currently offered to solar and wind farms, which would guarantee them minimum revenues.
The Treasury has also floated the idea of investments by the National Wealth Fund.
Whatever the answer, Starmer needs to get a move on, says one nuclear industry insider.
“When we speak to our investors they’re asking: ‘What tangible things is the Government really doing here?’
“The Sizewell C and the Rolls-Royce SMR decisions, those were actually really good for the broader industry because they actually showed this Government does believe in nuclear.
“But the Government can’t afford to finance every new nuclear project that we will need. Alternative routes to market are needed.”
On Wednesday, a spokesman for the ONR said it was seeking a “clear strategic steer from government” on how it should make decisions to speed up nuclear deployment.
“We welcome challenge and debate as a necessary part of a healthy regulatory system and remain committed to ensuring our regulation does not delay nuclear projects as we work hard to enable their safe delivery,” a spokesman added.
A government spokesman said ministers were “modernising outdated regulations to unlock a golden age of nuclear, securing thousands of good, skilled jobs and billions in investment”.

image.caption: Sir Keir Starmer on a visit to Hinkley Point, in Somerset. The PM wants Britain to embrace nuclear power
The decision to fund mini-reactors designed by Rolls-Royce have buoyed hopes about Labour’s commitment to nuclear

author: Matt Oliver

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2025/09.title: Palestine Action co-founder claims ban on group is discrimination
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2025/09.subtitle: Huda Ammori’s lawyers argue proscription will have ‘significant impact’ on UK Palestinians
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2025/09.text:
Lawyers for Palestine Action’s co-founder have claimed that the ban on the group is discriminatory.
Huda Ammori, 31, is seeking a judicial review of the measure, and her lawyers have cited equality laws in her fight to get it overturned.
Yvette Cooper, the former home secretary, outlawed the group following an alleged attack on two Voyager aircraft at RAF Brize Norton on June 20.
The ban, which began on July 5, means membership of the organisation, or support for it, is a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
Ms Ammori’s lawyers told the Court of Appeal that Ms Cooper “failed to have regard” for Palestinians living in Britain, who they said had protected characteristics under the Equality Act.
More than 1,600 alleged Palestine Action supporters have been arrested since the ban came into place, according to the campaign group Defend Our Juries.
Mr Justice Chamberlain, a High Court judge, later allowed Ms Ammori to proceed with a challenge over the ban after finding that two arguments put forward on her behalf were “reasonably arguable”. The Home Office is challenging this decision at the Court of Appeal.
Addressing a panel of judges on Thursday, Blinne Ni Ghralaigh K, one of Ms Ammori’s lawyers, said: “[Our] first point is the Secretary of State failed to have regard at all to the particular impacts on the Palestinian Community as a community in Britain.”
She went on to say the proscription of Palestine Action was going to have a “significant impact” on the Palestinians in the UK, which could include “disincentivising free speech” and “their [Palestinians’] place in British society”.
Legal documents also compared the ban on the pro-Palestine group with that of other Left-wing groups such as Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion.
Submissions handed to the court by her lawyers read: “Without adequate equalities advice, the SSHD [Home Secretary] failed to have due regard to…the measure’s negative discriminatory effect against Palestinians or those in support of the Palestinian cause…or indeed against PA itself, by comparison with other direct action groups which…. ‘employ direct-action tactics similar to those’ of PA…but which hold different political beliefs and which are not proscribed (e.g. Extinction Rebellion, Just Stop Oil).
“Members of the Palestinian community face acute, unique equalities impacts as a result of the proscription, distinct from the broader concerns of those who ‘support the Palestinian cause’.
“The [Home Secretary] failed to give due regard to this community. The reference to ‘smaller communities in the UK’ in the CIA [Community Impact Assessment] has nothing to do with equalities impacts.
“However, the NCCT also acknowledge that there will be a range of smaller communities in the UK concerned that [the proscription] demonstrates a lack of support for the Palestinian cause, which is likely to increase anti-government sentiment.
“This does not begin to constitute consideration of the equalities impacts on those minority communities, including (but not limited to) the Palestinian community.”
However, Sir James Eadie KC, for the Home Office, argued that it was “pretty obvious” that Ms Cooper and her colleagues were “considering Palestinian issues”.
Discussing a community impact assessment carried out ahead of the ban, Sir James said there were “references to communities, which at the very least include the Palestinian community”, such as British Muslims.
Sir James later told the court there was “nothing exceptional” about Ms Ammori’s case, adding: “It would require an exceptional case before judicial review would cut in.
“If a claimant invites the court to exercise its discretion to entertain an application for judicial review in circumstances where Parliament itself has provided a statutory process intended to cater for the substantive challenges that could be made to the thing that affects the individual, it is for the claimant to show an exceptional case.”
In a statement ahead of Thursday’s appeal, Ms Ammori said: “It’s deeply troubling that the previous home secretary decided to try to stop a full legal review of her widely condemned decision to ban a protest group as a ‘terrorist’ organisation for the first time in British history.”
“A successful appeal would not only shield an unlawful ban from scrutiny – it would deny justice to thousands of people whose fundamental free speech rights have been violated by this ban.”
Raza Husain KC, who also represents Ms Ammori, said her client should be able to bring more arguments to the full hearing which is due in November.
The barrister said it was “at least arguable” that Ms Cooper had not acted for national security reasons, but for other, “improper” purposes, and that Ms Ammori should be able to challenge the Home Office over potentially failing to properly consider the discriminatory effect against Palestinians or people who support Palestine.
A judgment will be handed down at a later date.

image.caption: Following the ban, membership and support of Palestine Action can carry sentences of up to 14 years in prison
Huda Ammori, 31, is seeking a judicial review of the ban on Palestine Action
Last year, Palestine Action released footage of an activist spraying red paint and slashing a painting of Lord Arthur James Balfour at Trinity College, Cambridge

author: Fiona Parker
